title: The Alembic
subtitle: Data Visualization II · multiple mappings + solvent selection
story: You wake to alarm bells and a floor tilting under your boots — and a cold, spreading mark on your forearm, where something alien slipped under your skin as you came aboard. This is the Alembic, a brass-and-canvas airship gone adrift over a world of floating islands and green alien sky, and she is listing further by the minute, sliding toward the crags. Two problems share one answer: the ship's medicine and its control-locks both run off the same rack of solvents, so the one liquid that kills the thing in your arm is the same one that frees the ship's seized helm. Cure yourself, work your way through the ship to the engine that mixes the cure, then climb to the bridge and take the wheel — because the only way to steer the Alembic clear is to read your way home by the stars.
enterLabel: Check the mark on your arm →

done.title: The cure, and the ship set free
done.body: You've named it — the one solvent that won't mix with water, sits at middling polarity, and rides lighter than water. You tip a measured charge into the dispensary funnel: the cold spreading stops dead across the lesion, and the same solvent floods the ship's lock-hydraulics. Every seized control shudders loose — the helm is alive again, up on the bridge, waiting for a bearing.

escapeDone.title: Home by the stars
escapeDone.body: Up in the crow's nest the captain's astrolabe turns under your hands — three plates for one sky — and only a single star holds its place in the homeward house through every one of them. You set the wheel to its bearing. The Alembic answers, banking off the black crags and climbing into clean night, and glides toward the one safe island the whole sky agreed upon — cured, and flying, the mark on your arm already fading.

rooms.title: The apothecary bay
rooms.technique: read one property of the solvents; the mapping still-kit
rooms.designNote: TEACHING ROOM 1 — THE APOTHECARY BAY. Story: the player finds the cold alien lesion on their arm and a brass field TEST-KIT; the ship's medicine and its door-locks both run on the same solvent rack, so curing themselves and reaching the helm are one problem. This station reads the FIRST property of the cure (e.g. it must NOT mix with water — read miscible_with_water). Per the pre/post principle, pose it as a MULTI-VARIABLE MAPPING plot (map several solvent properties to aesthetics, read one off) — NOT a single-column filter — mirroring hospital's question style. Solving narrows the cure AND releases the door onward. ALSO the home of the brass mapping DIAL (obj_dial): flipping it sets gameState.mapping to a sigil (m1/m2/m3); its effect isn't explained or visible here — it drives the crow's-nest chart much later (Riven: a control changing a distant display). Exact MCQ/plot TBD in the teaching-room design pass.

authoring.scenePrompt: This is a panorama. A 360-degree view from the centre of the apothecary bay of a steampunk airship, the room wrapping continuously all the way around so the left and right edges meet seamlessly. Along one wall, brass racks of small glass solvent vials above a workbench with a copper distillation still and a BRASS FIELD TEST-KIT — a boxy analytical instrument with a small glowing glass screen showing a faint scatter-plot. On one side an open riveted companion-ladder climbs UP to a hatch onto the deep night sky of the weather deck; on the other, an open floor-hatch with a ladder descends DOWN into the dim cargo hold. Around the rest of the bay: gauges, coiled copper pipes, hanging oil lanterns, a wooden apothecary chest, and portholes onto a dark, green-tinged night sky with the first stars out over floating islands. Steady warm brass lamplight against the night beyond the portholes, brass-and-verdigris palette, drifting steam, film grain, richly detailed. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text.

question.prompt: Your test-kit's first panel reacts only to solvents that will not mix with water. How does whether a solvent mixes with water relate to its polarity — which statement is true?
options: Solvents that mix with water tend to sit at LOWER relative polarity
Solvents that mix with water tend to sit at HIGHER relative polarity
Whether a solvent mixes with water is unrelated to its polarity
Every solvent that mixes with water is denser than water
Only chlorinated solvents mix with water
Solvents that mix with water tend to be less dense

feedback.correct: Right — the water-mixers cluster toward higher polarity. So your cure, which won't mix with water, is one of the lower-polarity, water-shy solvents. The kit's first light goes green and the bay door unlatches.
wrong: Colour the points by miscible_with_water and compare where each colour sits along relative_polarity.
Look again — the water-mixing group sits toward the HIGHER-polarity end.
The polar solvents are the ones that dissolve into water.

rooms.title: The cargo hold
rooms.technique: facet_wrap(~category) — the taught trap: the pooled polarity rule breaks inside the alcohols
rooms.designNote: TEACHING ROOM 3 — DEEP IN THE HOLD. THE TAUGHT TRAP (reworked 2026-07-22). Story: the test-kit now faces the cure's own family. Room 1 established the pooled rule — water-mixers are the more polar solvents. Here the player facets by category and looks inside the ALCOHOLS, where that rule collapses: 2-propanol mixes with water yet is LESS polar (0.546) than 1-butanol (0.586), which doesn't; polarity can't separate the alcohols, but density (chain length) does, cleanly. Load-bearing — the cure (1-butanol) is itself one of the polar-but-immiscible exceptions. Dark, cavernous hold; the plot lives on the laptop. Mirrors hospital's room-3 facet subversion. Verified vs solvents.csv; correct = idx 2.

question.prompt: Room 1's rule — the solvents that mix with water are the more polar ones — was read across the whole rack. Now look inside one family, the alcohols, coloured by whether they mix with water: what actually separates the alcohols that mix from those that don't?
options: The same rule holds — the alcohols that mix are simply the more polar ones
Nothing separates them — every alcohol mixes with water
Polarity barely separates them; it's the heavier, longer-chain alcohols that stop mixing, so density tells them apart — not polarity
The alcohols that mix are the denser ones
Only chlorinated alcohols fail to mix
The alcohols that don't mix are simply the least polar ones

feedback.correct: Exactly — inside the alcohols the polarities overlap, but density (chain length) decides. Only two polar alcohols refuse to mix with water: 1-butanol and 1-octanol — and your cure is one of them. The companionway to the bridge grinds open.
wrong: Split the rack into small multiples by category and look only at the alcohol panel; colour by miscible_with_water, and check whether polarity actually separates the two colours.
Inside the alcohols the polarities overlap — two that don't mix sit right among ones that do. Compare their densities instead.
The alcohols that refuse to mix are the heavier, longer-chain ones — read density, not polarity.

rooms.technique: the full three-condition solvent selection (graded Q3), administered at the dispensary; mints the Canvas code
rooms.designNote: BOSS (graded -> Canvas code) — THE ENGINE ROOM / DISPENSARY. Combining all three readings, the player names the ONE solvent that is immiscible with water, relative_polarity nearest 0.6, AND density below water (Data-Vis-II Q3). Verified answer: 1-BUTANOL. It is mixed and poured at the dispensary console, curing the lesion AND flooding the ship's lock-hydraulics so the seized helm frees. availableWhen {allSolved room1/room2/room3} gates the boss puzzle to this room. Ends the ANALYSIS objective + mints the code.

rooms.title: The crow's nest
rooms.technique: escape — read the dial-driven star-plates (multiple mappings)
rooms.designNote: ESCAPE part 1 — THE CROW'S NEST (deep night, high on the mast, 'see the whole', very Riven). STAR REDESIGN 2026-07-22 (was solvent charts). The captain's star-astrolabe (obj_chart, a mapview) shows a field of NAMED STARS under whichever plate the room-1 astrolabe plate-dial selects (m1/m2/m3) as a pre-rendered PNG. Each plate projects the same stars a different way; the Anchor (homeward house) is marked on every plate. Exactly one star — SOLIRA — holds the Anchor across all three plates; its NAME is the helm lock. The star-log clue (obj_starlog) names the Anchor + the method, not the answer. Fully data-free (no solvents). PNGs + answer from nest/make_starchart.py; equal-length star names keep the lock a fixed length. The plate-dial is co-located here beside the astrolabe (moved out of room1 so there's no cross-ship back-nav during the escape); the player turns it, reads each plate, takes the intersection → SOLIRA → helm.

It is deep, clear night up here above the cloud. Ahead, the captain's great brass STAR-ASTROLABE on a swivel mount — a tall ringed instrument with a large engraved circular star-plate — and beside it a heavy BRASS PLATE-DIAL with three engraved marks and a needle for turning the astrolabe to a new plate; a chart table holds an open leather star-log and a spyglass. A railed ratline and ladder lead DOWN the mast to the weather deck below. All around, the railing gives onto an immense night sky blazing with stars over dark floating islands far below, rigging lines rising to the gas-bag above, a glowing signal lantern, a windsock snapping. Cold, constant starlight and warm brass highlights, wind-torn cloud, film grain, richly detailed. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text.

plannedHotspots.note: DIAL — astrolabe plate-dial (key 'mapping', 3 states ◈/⬢/✶). Co-located with the astrolabe; sets which star-plate obj_chart shows.

plannedHotspots.label: The captain's star-astrolabe
plannedHotspots.caption: The astrolabe's plate turns and the star field redraws — the same sky under a different projection each time, the Anchor marked on every face. Stars drift from plate to plate; the one that holds the Anchor through all three faces is your bearing home.
plannedHotspots.empty: The astrolabe's plate-ring is unset — the stars won't show. Turn the plate-dial beside it to choose a face of the sky.
plannedHotspots.note: MAPVIEW keyed on 'mapping' — three star-plate PNGs (nest/map_m{1,2,3}.png). Anchor marked on every plate; SOLIRA is the only star holding it across all three.

plannedHotspots.label: The captain's star-log
plannedHotspots.body: Open to a marked page, the captain's hand: “Steer always by the Anchor — the house high to the north-east that every plate of the astrolabe shares. Stars wander from face to face, but one alone keeps the Anchor through all three. That star is our bearing home; set the helm to its name.”

rooms.title: The bridge
rooms.technique: escape — set the invariant star's bearing at the helm to steer home
rooms.designNote: ESCAPE part 2 — THE BRIDGE (the helm; the finish). The helm bearing-keypad (obj_lock, answer SOLIRA, len 6) is DEAD until the cure has cycled (availableWhen {solved boss} + lockedBody). Enter the invariant star's name read off the astrolabe in the nest, then take the wheel (the forward 'Take the wheel' door, requires obj_lock, no `to`) -> escapeDone. The helm lives on the bridge, not a captain's cabin.

rooms.entry: You step onto the bridge. The great wheel waits at the helm, a bearing-keypad at the binnacle beside it, tall windows onto the dark floating crags rushing past. Set her course, and take her home.

feedback.correct: The name rings true — the plate-ring spins home and the door to the helm clicks open. The one star that held the Anchor through every face of the sky.
feedback.wrong: The rings grind and reset. That star wanders; it is not our bearing home.
